subsystems.name: Orbital reflector array
subsystems.role: collects sunlight in space and redirects it toward a construction site on a planetary surface.

subsystems.name: Beam targeting and relay optics
subsystems.role: focuses the reflected sunlight into a tight spot and keeps it aimed as the target moves.

subsystems.name: Regolith handling system
subsystems.role: excavates, transports and spreads raw regolith in controlled layers.
parts: gantry or robotic arm for deposition

subsystems.name: Sintering head and thermal control
subsystems.role: receives the concentrated beam and scans it across the regolith to melt or sinter it without over-evaporating.

subsystems.name: Power and thermal management
subsystems.role: keeps the orbital mirrors and ground equipment operating through lunar day and night.
parts: radioisotope or fission power units on the surface

subsystems.name: Structure verification
subsystems.role: checks that each sintered layer is sound before the next is added.
parts: sample return or in-situ mechanical testers

buildSteps.title: Survey and site preparation
buildSteps.detail: A robotic mission maps a flat area, measures regolith depth and composition, and clears loose rocks so that layers can be spread evenly.

buildSteps.title: Deploy the orbital mirror
buildSteps.detail: A large lightweight reflector — either a single gossamer mirror or a constellation of smaller ones — is launched and assembled in a polar or Sun-synchronous orbit, where it can see the site for long periods.

buildSteps.title: Land ground equipment
buildSteps.detail: Excavators, a gantry or robotic arm, a sintering head with sensors, and a power source are delivered to the site and tested.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the beam
buildSteps.detail: The orbital mirror focuses sunlight onto a small test patch. Operators measure spot size, temperature and heating rate, then adjust pointing and focus to achieve uniform sintering at around 1000–1200 °C.

buildSteps.title: Deposit the first layer
buildSteps.detail: The regolith handler spreads a thin, even layer — typically a few millimetres to centimetres thick — over the build area.

buildSteps.title: Sinter the layer
buildSteps.detail: The concentrated beam is scanned across the layer. Pyrometers feed back to the control computer, which modulates scan speed and beam power to melt grain surfaces together without boiling the regolith.

buildSteps.title: Repeat layer by layer
buildSteps.detail: Fresh regolith is deposited on the cooled, solid layer and sintered again. Repeating this builds walls, pads or domes additively, with each pass fusing to the one below.

buildSteps.title: Finish and inspect
buildSteps.detail: The structure is allowed to cool slowly to avoid cracking. Lidar and acoustic tests check for voids or weak bonds; defects can be repaired by local re-sintering.

buildSteps.title: Commission the structure
buildSteps.detail: The finished object — a landing pad, radiation shield, road or habitat shell — is put into service, potentially with added sealing or outfitting.

prerequisites.tech: Concentrated solar sintering of lunar regolith
prerequisites.why: Laboratory experiments have melted and fused regolith simulant using focused sunlight and microwaves, but not yet on the Moon or at structural scale.
Deployable solar arrays and antennas exist, but kilometre-scale mirrors require new packaging, assembly and control techniques.
Rovers and landers have moved small amounts of soil on the Moon and Mars, but continuous mining and spreading at construction scale is unproven.
Laser communications and ground-based solar concentrators demonstrate fine pointing, but holding a high-power beam on a moving surface target for hours is new.
Radioisotope heaters and small fission concepts exist, but powering excavators, gantries and sensors through the 14-day lunar night at scale is unsolved.
Thin-film reflectors and coatings survive space radiation and ultraviolet light in current spacecraft, though scaling to very large areas remains a challenge.

pathway.milestone: Laboratory demonstrations sinter lunar regolith simulant with concentrated light and microwaves
pathway.unlocks: Proof that regolith can be fused without additives, and basic data on temperatures and strengths.

pathway.milestone: Small lander-mounted mirror sinters a test object on the lunar surface
pathway.unlocks: Real-environment data on vacuum, dust and thermal cycling for sintering.

pathway.milestone: Orbital mirror demonstrates beam delivery to a surface target
pathway.unlocks: Validation of long-distance power beaming and pointing control.

pathway.milestone: Robotic construction of a simple structure such as a landing pad or radiation wall
pathway.unlocks: A repeatable additive construction process for lunar infrastructure.

pathway.milestone: Full-scale habitats or asteroid structures built by planetary-scale sintering
pathway.unlocks: Large pressurised volumes and shielding made from local materials, reducing launch mass from Earth.
